title: Emotions bubble over at budget hearing on developmental disabilities service cuts
summary: The hearing on $150 million in proposed cuts to the  Developmental Disabilities Administration was mostly dry, until recipients and family members began telling their personal stories, and two years of fears and frustration bubbled over.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters February 26, 2026

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters February 26, 2026

The hearing room was packed, but the hearing itself was mostly dry, with legislative anaylsts and Maryland Health Department officials going back and forth on the reasoning and the details of a proposed $150 million cut to the budget for the Developmental Disabilities Administration.

That was until Del. Dana Jones (D-Anne Arundel) shared the conversations that she said she kept returning to as she prepared for Thursday’s budget hearing.

“There have been several conversations that I’ve been able to have with constituents that continue to ring in my ears,” said Jones. “And one that kept coming up … was the fight that every parent feels.

“Finding out what’s wrong, seeing specialist after specialist, genetic doctors, every doctor out there. Fighting insurance, fighting school systems, fighting doctors,” she said. “That was so heavy on my heart, because it was echoed … by all of the folks who I met with.”

It sparked a round of applause from the crowd in the joint hearing room in the Department of Legislative Services, and set the stage for emotional testimony from DDA clients and family members, as two years of anguish, frustration and fear due to budget cuts proposed for the agency bubbled over.

Gov. Wes Moore’s (D) proposed budget would cut $150 million from the agency, as the state works to close a projected $1.5 billion budget shortfall. Moore proposed several “cost containment measures” to make the cuts and to rein in “unsustainable” spending at the DDA. Advocates note that the state reductions would actually equate to $300 million in cuts, as the state funds are tied to matching federal dollars under Medicaid waivers.

It’s the second year that advocates have come to Annapolis with deep concerns about proposed budget cuts.

Last year, Moore’s initial budget proposed more than $400 million in cuts to the DDA, as the state was struggling to close a $3 billion budget gap. Subsequent lobbying and work with lawmakers brought the final cuts last year to about $164 million.

Advocates say access to services has already been affected by last year’s cuts, and that more cuts now would be devastating to one of Maryland’s most vulnerable populations. In addition, advocates continue to face communication challenges with state officials when problems arise with their coverage.

The DDA administers Medicaid waivers that let Marylanders with developmental disabilities receive a wide variety of services, from live-in caregiver support to transportation, respite care, employment services and more.

In fiscal 2025, nearly 15,200 people received services from a community provider, an organization that provides disability care; another 3,900 people chose the self-directed care model, in which funding recipient or their family directly hires caregivers.

Advocates say the proposed cuts would threaten the wages for one-on-one support staff and other positions that help those with the highest need.

Maryland Health Secretary Meena Seshamani said the proposed cost-containment measures are necessary for the sustainability of the waiver program and ensure that federal officials allow it to continue.

“We are in a challenging time,” she said during the budget hearing. “The fiscal year 2027 budget sustainability items are needed to keep the Medicaid waiver program approved, funded and operational.

“Without the sustainability actions, the state would face a threat to its Medicaid waiver and escalating deficits – threatening provider stability, service continuity, and a waitlist that continues to grow without moving people into services,” Seshamani said.

But the policy debate was no match for the personal stories of recipients.

Liz Eisner’s 25-year-old daughter, Ingrid, has autism and goes to adult residential programs and day services with a community provider. Eisner said that being with the community provider has allowed Ingrid to become more independent — doing laundry, helping clean her apartment and overcoming her fear of going up and down stairs.

“If DDA funding is reduced, and if Ingrid loses her one-on-one supports, all of her progress will be at risk,” Eisner said. “Please protect the health, safety and dignity of people like my daughter.”

Emotions boiled over for Angela Noppenberger, the mother of two teenage children with developmental disabilities, who described the challenges she faced working through the appeals process with the DDA after it denied some of their services. Noppenberger said the appeal process “is very stressful and taxing on families” — even for her, a longtime social worker in Baltimore City. That was not lost on Jones.

Advocates: Services, workers at risk from second year of developmental disabilities budget cuts

“It sounded, even with your 24-year history of being a social worker … that this was many times overwhelming and untenable,” Jones said. “Am I misclassifying your family’s thoughts?”

“You are not, Delegate Jones,” she said, taking a breath before starting to cry through her testimony. “Our personal supports save us. If I did not have my personal supports, I could not take care of my children.

“They could not live with us. Could you imagine not tucking your children in — 19 and 16 — into bed because you could not handle them?” she asked. “Our personal supports … they help us so that this does not happen. And we will lose them if we have to cut their budgets.”

Tracie Feron’s son Connor, 30, has autism and other medical conditions that require round-the-clock care. She said his self-directed support services have improved his quality of life and are helping him learn how to communicate through “augmentative and alternative communication.”

“One letter at a time, one word at a time,” she said, holding up a laminated page with the alphabet on it. “Through self-direction, we were able to ensure consistent, trained support staff who believed in his competence and helped to build this skill.

“When rates are cut or reduced, we lose qualified staff. When we lose staff, we lose stability,” she told the committee. “With proposed budget and wage cuts, individuals will be harmed … these are not abstract numbers. These are human lives.”

She then asked Connor if he would like to speak. He pointed to ‘Y’, ‘E’ and ‘S’ on the letter board. She asked him to describe why self-directed services were important to him.

“I’m heard,” he spelled out, by pointing to the letters on the page, which Tracie relayed to the room.
